Quote/Description (Actual Sentiment — No: USA (Nationwide)
Source URL: 78% of drivers said they don't always trust their mechanics. / Only 17% of respondents felt like they're always charged fairly for car repairs. / About 5 in 6 (83%) people said they sometimes or always consult someone they know to double-check mechanics' recommendations.
column9: ConsumerAffairs survey of 1,000 US drivers (Aug 2023, Pollfish). Core finding: trust deficit is structural and widespread. Drivers' go-to resolution is to consult informal social networks — friends and family — who have no more information than they do. Triad: Financial Cost (only 17% feel fairly charged); Information Asymmetry (83% seek outside verification because they cannot evaluate what they were told).

column9: Jerry survey of 1,431 US vehicle owners (May 2023). Car repairs produce more confusion and distrust than medical bills, home repairs, or legal/accounting services. After shops, the most-used information source is friends and family. Triad: Financial Cost (majority feel overcharged); Information Asymmetry (no trusted independent source to evaluate what services are needed or what they should cost).

This means that a good mechanic that can troubleshoot a problem in 0.5 hours may charge significantly less than a clueless mechanic that spends 2 days swapping parts to figure it out.
Context and Triad Activation: Undated (written ~1997-2010)
column9: Former 15-year industry mechanic explains the structural incentive problem from the inside: flat-rate pay rewards volume of flagged repairs; honest diagnostics are penalized. Important provider-side mirror on all three sub-dimensions: vocabulary failures are not malicious — they emerge from a professional frame that assumes shared knowledge. Implication and urgency gaps emerge because experienced mechanics carry pattern recognition in their bodies that is invisible to car owners. Triad: Information Asymmetry (structural — the incentive system itself produces communication gaps); Financial Cost (good fast diagnosis may charge less than bad slow guess-work — opaque to consumer).

Car owner didn't understand what a 'solder connection' was or why the diagnostic price changed post-warranty. Forum responders confirmed the price change was improper and the diagnosis should have been applied to the repair. column9: California car owner (Maria) paid $1,400 for a transmission solenoid replacement and fluid flush. Car continued to exhibit the same symptoms. Brought back; shop said 'additional issues' would cost $900 more. When she asked why the first repair hadn't worked, she got a shrug and 'parts wear out.' She received no written explanation. Decision-Architecture Failure at maximum: the car owner processed the information but could not build any evaluative framework because the shop's own explanation shifted. Triad: Information Asymmetry (repair failure unexplained — no bridge from action to outcome); Financial Cost ($1,400 spent on a repair that didn't work).
